group.title: Talking and messages
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A conversation you have by ringing someone on a mobile or landline.
examples: I need to make a quick {phone call}.
wrong: He made a phone call by writing a letter.

words.meaning: A short piece of writing sent from one mobile to another.
examples: She sent me a {text message} to say she was late.
wrong: I listened to his text message on the radio.

words.meaning: A system that records a spoken message when you can’t answer the phone.
examples: He didn’t answer, so I left a message on his {voicemail}.
wrong: I read the voicemail in the newspaper.

words.meaning: To record or write something for a person who is not there.
examples: She’s out, but you can {leave a message}.
wrong: He left a message by talking to her face to face.

words.meaning: To end a phone call by putting down or switching off the phone.
examples: She said goodbye and {hung up}.
wrong: He hung up the phone to start the call.

words.meaning: To ring someone again, or ring a person who tried to reach you.
examples: I’m busy now, so I’ll {call back} later.
wrong: I called back before she had ever phoned me.

words.meaning: To press the numbers on a phone to call someone.
examples: In an emergency, {dial} the police number.
wrong: He dialed the number by sending an email.

words.meaning: A ring on your phone that you did not answer in time.
examples: I had three {missed calls} from my mom.
wrong: A missed call is a call you answered and enjoyed.

words.meaning: A phone or online talk where people can see each other on a screen.
examples: We have a {video call} with Grandma every Sunday.
wrong: On the video call we couldn’t see or hear each other at all.

words.meaning: An online conversation with several people at the same time.
examples: The class has a {group chat} for homework questions.
wrong: Our group chat has only one person in it.

words.meaning: To talk in a friendly, relaxed way.
examples: We {chatted} about our holidays over coffee.
wrong: They chatted for an hour without saying a word.

words.meaning: To speak very quietly so only one person can hear.
examples: She {whispered} the secret in my ear.
wrong: He whispered so loudly that the whole street heard.

words.meaning: To speak or write about something briefly.
examples: Did she {mention} her new job?
wrong: He mentioned the party by saying nothing about it.

words.meaning: To talk about something with others to share ideas.
examples: We {discussed} the plan at the meeting.
wrong: They discussed the problem without talking to each other.

words.meaning: To answer someone in speech or writing.
examples: Please {reply} to my email soon.
wrong: She replied to the letter before she got it.

words.meaning: An answer or reaction to something.
examples: I’m still waiting for a {response} to my letter.
wrong: His response came before I asked the question.

words.meaning: To tell many people about something officially.
examples: The pilot {announced} that we would land soon.
wrong: She announced the news by keeping it a secret.

words.meaning: A public statement giving information.
examples: There was an {announcement} about the late train.
wrong: The announcement was a secret nobody heard.

words.meaning: A flat paper cover you put a letter in.
examples: Write the address on the {envelope}.
wrong: I drank my tea from an envelope.

words.meaning: A small sticker you buy and put on a letter to send it.
examples: You need a {stamp} to post this card.
wrong: He put a stamp on his foot to send the letter.

words.meaning: A card with a picture on one side, sent without an envelope.
examples: She sent us a {postcard} from Paris.
wrong: A postcard is a phone call you make from a hotel.

words.meaning: To send a letter or package by post.
examples: I’ll {mail} the documents to you tomorrow.
wrong: He mailed the letter by keeping it in his drawer.

words.meaning: The person who gets a letter, message or gift.
examples: Check the name of the {recipient} before you send it.
wrong: The recipient is the person who writes and sends the email.

words.meaning: The person a letter or message comes from.
examples: The {sender}’s address is on the back of the envelope.
wrong: The sender is the person who receives the parcel.

words.meaning: A file sent together with an email.
examples: Please open the {attachment} to see the photos.
wrong: The attachment is the subject line of the email.

words.meaning: To contact someone by phone, letter or message.
examples: Please {get in touch} if you have any questions.
wrong: He got in touch by never calling or writing to us.

words.meaning: Polite chat about unimportant things, like the weather.
examples: We made {small talk} while we waited for the bus.
wrong: Their small talk was a long, serious talk about their problems.

words.meaning: To stop someone while they are speaking.
examples: Please don’t {interrupt} me when I’m talking.
wrong: She interrupted him by waiting until he finished.

words.meaning: To show a feeling or idea in words or actions.
examples: She {expressed} her thanks with a card.
wrong: He expressed his feelings by hiding them.

words.meaning: To move your head up and down, often to say yes.
examples: He {nodded} when I asked if he was ready.
wrong: She nodded to say no by shaking her head from side to side.

words.meaning: To give someone facts or news officially.
examples: Please {inform} us if your address changes.
wrong: They informed us by telling us nothing.

words.meaning: To call, write to or message someone.
examples: You can {contact} me by email.
wrong: She contacted him by never calling or writing.

words.meaning: To share information or feelings with others.
examples: Dolphins {communicate} with sounds.
wrong: They communicated by never sharing any ideas.

words.meaning: Words or actions used when you meet someone.
examples: "Hello" is a common {greeting}.
wrong: "Goodbye" is the greeting you use when you arrive.

words.meaning: The style of the letters a person makes with a pen.
examples: I can’t read his {handwriting}; it’s very messy.
wrong: Her handwriting is the voice she uses on the phone.

words.meaning: The short title of an email that shows what it is about.
examples: Write "Meeting" in the {subject line}.
wrong: The subject line is the last sentence of an email.

words.meaning: To send a message you received on to another person.
examples: I’ll {forward} his email to you.
wrong: She forwarded the email by deleting it.

words.meaning: To talk more loudly so people can hear you.
examples: Could you {speak up}? I can’t hear you.
wrong: Please speak up so nobody can hear you.

words.meaning: A way of pronouncing words that shows where you come from.
examples: She speaks English with a French {accent}.
wrong: His accent is the meaning of the words he says.

words.meaning: The strength of a phone’s connection to the network.
examples: I have no {signal} here, so I can’t call.
wrong: With a strong signal, my calls kept failing.
